Bias-Variance Decomposition Estimates bias and variance of a model using bootstrap resampling on synthetic data. Compares three models: constant (high bias), linear (good), and high-degree polynomial (high variance). Use this to diagnose whether poor performance is due to underfitting (high bias) or overfitting (high variance).

Bootstrap Model Comparison Compares two models using paired bootstrap resampling on the same test set. Computes the win rate: how often Model A is better than Model B across bootstrap samples. Use this to determine whether observed performance difference is statistically significant, or could be due to random variation in the test set.

Calibration Curve & Brier Score Evaluates classifier calibration by binning predicted probabilities and comparing observed frequency vs predicted probability. Also computes Brier score (MSE of predictions). Use this to detect overconfident models (predicted prob >> observed freq) or underconfident models. A well-calibrated classifier has observed ≈ predicted across bins.

Gaussian Naive Bayes Classifier Implements a Gaussian Naive Bayes classifier for continuous features. Assumes each feature is independently distributed as Gaussian given the class label. Use this for fast, interpretable classification on continuous data, especially when feature independence is a reasonable assumption.

Learning Curve Analysis Plots error vs training set size to assess model stability and data hunger. Verifies that training error increases and validation error decreases as training data grows, indicating the model has capacity to benefit from more data without overfitting. Use this to diagnose high bias (both curves high and flat) vs high variance (training low, validation high).

Lift & Gain Chart Computes cumulative gain (% of positives captured) and lift (gain / base rate) by decile. Lift > 1 indicates the model is better than random. Use this in marketing/targeting to quantify how much better a model ranks customers than random.

Precision-Recall Curve & Average Precision Computes PR curve by varying decision threshold on predicted scores. Average Precision (AP) summarizes the curve as area under the PR curve. Use this to evaluate binary classifiers, especially on imbalanced datasets where PR curve is more informative than ROC curve.

Rank Correlation (Spearman's rho & Kendall's tau) Computes Spearman's rank correlation (Pearson on ranks) and Kendall's tau (proportion of concordant pairs). Autocovariance and Power Spectral Density (Periodogram). Periodogram = DFT of autocovariance function. For a signal with strong periodicity, the periodogram should show a peak at that frequency. We plant a periodic signal and verify the periodogram peaks at the correct frequency.

Dynamic Range Compression via Logarithm and μ-Law. Compress large dynamic range (e.g., audio amplitudes or intensity values) into a narrower range while preserving relative differences at small scales. Both log compression and μ-law compression should be invertible and reduce the dynamic range.

Peak Detection via Prominence. Find local maxima in a signal using prominence: height above the baseline (minimum of the valleys to the left and right). Detect planted peaks; reject noise bumps that don't meet prominence threshold.

Resampling and Interpolation. Upsample or downsample a time series via interpolation. Demonstrate linear interpolation and nearest-neighbor. On smooth signals, linear should outperform nearest-neighbor (lower RMSE).

Savitzky-Golay Filter (Local Polynomial Smoothing). Fit a low-order polynomial (e.g., quadratic) to a rolling window. Smoother than moving-average and preserves peak heights better than moving-average. We verify that SG filter preserves peak heights while moving-average attenuates them.
Discrete Event Simulation: service desk with event queue. Uses heapq for event-driven simulation. Verifies conservation: arrivals == served + still-in-system. Also shows waits grow with utilization.

Kelly Criterion: optimal betting fraction for long-run log-growth. Kelly fraction f* = (p*b - q) / b where p = win prob, q = loss prob, b = odds. Overbetting (2x Kelly) produces lower median terminal wealth: the classic warning.
M/M/1 Queue: verify Little's Law and analytic formulas. Simulates an M/M/1 queue (Poisson arrivals, exponential service). Verifies Little's Law: L ≈ λW. Also compares to analytic M/M/1 formulas.

Monte Carlo VaR & ES: Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall on returns. Computes Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) on heavy-tailed synthetic returns. Verifies ES >= VaR always, and empirical exceedance rate ≈ alpha (confidence level).

Newsvendor Problem: optimal stock at critical fractile. Optimal order quantity is the critical fractile of demand. Profit at optimal quantity exceeds over/under stocking, measured over many seeded days.

Q-Learning on Gridworld: reach value iteration policy through off-policy learning. Tabular Q-learning on the same 4x4 gridworld. After sufficient episodes, Q-learning converges to the same policy as value iteration. Policies are compared directly.

Schelling Segregation: mild preference produces high global segregation. Agents prefer neighbors of same type with threshold >= 30%. Simulation shows high global segregation emerges from mild individual preference. Segregation measured before/after as ratio of same-type neighbors.

SIR Epidemic Model: discrete simulation of S-I-R dynamics. Discrete SIR: tracks susceptible, infected, recovered counts. Verifies conservation S + I + R = N every step, and validates theory: peak timing/height respond to beta, final size increases with R0.

Tornado Sensitivity: one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis. Simple profit model: profit = (revenue - cost - overhead). OAT sensitivity varies each input by +/- 10% and measures profit impact. Ranked bar (via sorted list) identifies the dominant driver.

Adaptive Simpson's rule: automatic step refinement via error estimation. Compares Simpson's estimate on [a, b] with two estimates on [a, c] and [c, b]. If error is acceptable, return result; else recurse. Typical result: O(h⁴) accuracy with far fewer function evals than fixed-step methods. Planted integral recovered; function eval count measured vs fixed Simpson.

Hybrid bisection–Newton root-finding for robustness. Combines bisection's guaranteed convergence with Newton's speed: bisect when Newton drift is detected, switch back when safe. Core claim: planted root recovered accurately even when Newton would diverge or miss the derivative.

Natural cubic spline: piecewise cubic interpolation with C² continuity. Solves tridiagonal system for interior knot second derivatives; uses them to define cubic polynomials on each segment. Core claim: C² continuity + smooth approximation. Planted function (sin curve) interpolated; values and derivatives recovered exactly at nodes, smooth between.

Forward Euler vs RK4: measure convergence order difference. Solves same ODE with both methods at successive step sizes; measures error vs h. Core claim: Euler is O(h), RK4 is O(h⁴). Planted ODE with known solution; measured convergence rates match theory, RK4 dominates at fine steps.

Fixed-point iteration: find x where g(x) = x. Equivalently solves f(x) = 0 by reformulating as g(x) = x where g(x) = x - f(x). Core claim: convergence speed depends on |g'(x*)|; contraction mapping guarantees. Planted fixed point recovered; measured iteration count vs theory (linear order).

Gauss–Legendre quadrature: optimal node placement for polynomial integration. Hardcoded nodes and weights for n=4 (integrates degree ≤7 polynomials exactly). Core claim: fewer function evals than trapezoid for smooth functions; exact on high-degree polynomials. Planted integral recovered; order verified vs explicit formula.

Richardson extrapolation: boost convergence order via linear combination. If F(h) ≈ L + C·h^p + O(h^(2p)) and the step is halved, then (2^p·F(h/2) - F(h))/(2^p - 1) ≈ L + O(h^(2p)) — the C·h^p term cancels because F(h/2) carries it scaled by (1/2)^p. Core claim: raises O(h^p) error to O(h^(2p)) without changing the method. Planted integral; error dropped to O(h^(2p)) verified. NOTE: the eliminatio

Fourth-order Runge–Kutta: standard explicit ODE integrator. Solves dy/dt = f(t, y) using 4-stage RK scheme with O(h⁵) local error. Core claim: high accuracy on smooth systems; verified vs analytic solutions. Planted ODE (exponential decay) integrated; solution recovered to tight tolerance.

Romberg integration: Richardson extrapolation on trapezoid rule. Generates a table of progressively refined trapezoid estimates, then extrapolates to higher-order accuracy. Core claim: O(h⁴) error for smooth integrand vs O(h²) from bare trapezoid. Planted integral recovered; order verified.

Secant method: Newton's speed without derivatives. Uses finite-difference slope from two prior points to approximate f'(x). Core claim: converges superlinearly (order ≈1.618) without explicit derivative. Planted root recovered; convergence order measured vs analytic predictions.

Accelerated failure time (AFT): log-linear regression on survival times. Model: log(T) = μ + β·x + σ·ε where T is survival time, x is covariate. Core claim: linear relationship recovered; AFT coefficient close to truth.

Censoring bias: ignoring censoring biases survival estimates downward. Demonstrated: comparing naive mean of observed times vs Kaplan-Meier estimate shows that censored data underestimates true mean survival time. Core claim: naive mean < KM mean; the difference is measured.

Competing risks: the naive 1−KM overestimates incidence; Aalen-Johansen is correct. With competing events, a common MISTAKE is to estimate the cumulative incidence of cause 1 as 1 − KM, where the cause-specific Kaplan-Meier treats every competing event (and censoring) as if it were independent right-censoring. That double-counts the people removed by the competing risk and OVERSTATES the incidence

Cox partial likelihood: semiparametric survival model for 2-covariate hazard. Estimates hazard ratios via Newton-Raphson on partial likelihood. Core claim: planted hazard ratios recovered from censored data; Newton steps converge. Planted survival times with true HR, censoring, and covariate structure.

Exponential reliability: MTBF and survival function from failure times. For constant hazard h(t) = λ, survival S(t) = exp(-λt) and MTBF = 1/λ. Core claim: MTBF estimated from sample, compared to true and to analytic.

Hazard-survival conversion: verify duality h(t) = -d/dt[log S(t)]. Given S(t) or h(t), derive the other and check consistency. Planted S(t), compute h(t), then reconstruct S(t) from h(t); verify round-trip.

Log-rank test: nonparametric test for equality of survival curves. Compares two groups via observed vs expected events under null hypothesis (no group difference). Core claim: two different groups detected; identical groups not flagged as different.

Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard: nonparametric estimate from event times. H(t) = Σ d_i / y_i where d_i = events at time i, y_i = at-risk count. Core claim: cumulative hazard monotone increasing; verified vs Kaplan-Meier.

System reliability: series vs parallel from component reliabilities. Series: all components must work → R_sys = R1 · R2 · ... · Rn. Parallel: at least one must work → R_sys = 1 - (1-R1)·(1-R2)·...·(1-Rn). Core claim: system reliability computed correctly; verified vs simulation.

Weibull MLE: maximum-likelihood estimation of shape k and scale λ (uncensored). For iid Weibull data the log-likelihood is ℓ(k,λ) = n·ln k − n·k·ln λ + (k−1)·Σ ln t_i − Σ (t_i/λ)^k. Profiling out λ = (Σ t_i^k / n)^(1/k) leaves a single equation in k: 1/k + (1/n)Σ ln t_i − (Σ t_i^k ln t_i)/(Σ t_i^k) = 0, solved here by Newton-Raphson. This is the actual MLE (not a log-log probability-plot regressio

Count-Min Sketch for Frequency Estimation Core idea: A streaming data structure using hash functions to estimate item frequencies with bounded error. Memory-efficient alternative to exact counts. When to use: You have a massive stream and need approximate frequency estimates with formal error bounds, especially for detecting heavy hitters.

Online Covariance & Correlation via Welford's Method Core idea: Update mean, variance, and covariance in a single pass via numerically-stable incremental formulas. Matches batch computation to machine precision. When to use: You have streaming data and need covariance/correlation, or want numerically stable alternatives to naive summation.

Online Stochastic Gradient Descent Classifier Core idea: Train a logistic regressor in a single pass over a stream via SGD, updating weights with each sample. Should converge close to batch solution on separable data. When to use: Data is too large to fit in memory, or you need to update models continuously as new data arrives (online learning).

P² Quantile Estimator (Jain & Chlamtac, 1985) — streaming quantiles in O(1) memory. The REAL P² algorithm: exactly FIVE markers track (min, p/2, p, (1+p)/2, max). Each new observation shifts marker positions; when a marker drifts from its desired position, its height is adjusted by PIECEWISE-PARABOLIC (P²) interpolation, falling back to linear when the parabola would break marker ordering. No buff

Page-Hinkley Test for Streaming Drift Detection Core idea: Monitor cumulative sum of (residuals - threshold) to detect if the distribution has shifted. High positive sum indicates upward drift; reset if drift detected. When to use: You're monitoring a stream metric and need early warning when it changes (e.g., system latency, error rate, model performance degradation).

Sliding Window Min/Max via Monotonic Deque Core idea: Maintain a deque of indices whose values are monotone. Each new element replaces non-competitive elements in O(1) amortized time. Verify against brute-force. When to use: You need sliding window min/max on a stream efficiently, or want to verify correctness of a deque-based implementation.

Space-Saving Algorithm for Top-K Heavy Hitters Core idea: Maintain exactly k counters for the top-k most frequent items seen so far. When a new item arrives, either increment an existing counter or replace the smallest one. When to use: You need the top-k most frequent items from a stream with minimal memory (only k counters, not a full frequency table).

Streaming Histogram with Bin Merging Core idea: Maintain a fixed-size histogram on a stream. When bins exceed the limit, merge adjacent bins to free space. Trade-off: quantile estimates have bounded error. When to use: You need a histogram summary of streaming data with bounded memory, or want to understand the accuracy/memory trade-off in streaming histogram algorithms.

Streaming k-means (Online Clustering) Core idea: Update cluster centroids incrementally as data streams in, without storing all points. On slowly-drifting data, centroids track the evolution. When to use: You have a streaming data source and need real-time clustering that adapts to slowly-changing data distributions.

Weighted Reservoir Sampling (A-Res Algorithm) Core idea: Sample k items from a weighted stream such that inclusion probability is proportional to item weight. A-Res: use u^(1/w) as sort key. When to use: You have a stream of weighted items and need a representative sample where rare (high-weight) items are more likely to appear.

Character n-gram language identification: distinguish languages via bigram profiles. Builds character bigram frequencies; compares via distance. Core claim: true language matched; false language rejected. Planted English vs pseudo-lang.

Complement Naive Bayes: robust on imbalanced text via the negative-class model. Vanilla multinomial NB scores class c with log P(c) + Σ f_w·log θ_{c,w}. Under heavy class imbalance the log-prior term drags ambiguous documents toward the majority class. Porter stemmer: rule-based morphological analysis for English word stemming. Reduces words to root form via suffix removal rules. Core claim: canonical test pairs stem correctly; planted words recover their stems.

Sentence boundary detection: split text at sentence ends despite abbreviations. Detects end-of-sentence punctuation (. ! ?) while NOT splitting on the periods inside common abbreviations (Dr., Mr., St., …). Core claim: abbreviation periods are protected; real sentence ends are split.

Soundex: phonetic encoding for name matching and fuzzy search. Maps names to 4-char code (1 letter + 3 digits) based on pronunciation. Core claim: known name pairs match (same code); dissimilar names differ.

TextRank: extract key sentences via graph centrality (damped power iteration). Builds a sentence similarity graph (Jaccard word overlap) and ranks sentences with the PageRank/TextRank recurrence, including the damping factor that keeps the iteration from collapsing to a uniform tie: score_i = (1−d)/n + d · Σ_{j≠i} (w_ji / Σ_k w_jk) · score_j. Core claim: the "hub" sentence that shares words with t

TF-IDF vs BM25: compare relevance ranking on length-biased documents. BM25 dampens length bias (saturation on high-TF terms) whereas TF-IDF linear. Core claim: on variable-length docs, BM25 ranks short docs higher; measured.
Zipf's law: rank-frequency relationship in natural language. log(frequency) ∝ log(rank) with slope ≈ −1. Core claim: natural text follows Zipf; uniform text violates it. Fitted slope measured.

Bayesian linear regression: conjugate normal prior, known noise, closed-form posterior. Core idea: prior N(μ₀, Σ₀); likelihood N(y | Xβ, σ²I); posterior is N(μ_post, Σ_post) with closed-form updates. Posterior mean is between prior and OLS; variance shrinks with data. When to use: interpretable regression with uncertainty, small data, informative priors.

Bayesian two-segment changepoint: marginal-likelihood comparison over split points. Core idea: compare model evidence for no-change vs change-at-t; find planted change location; no-change data prefers single-segment model. When to use: quality control, structural break detection, time-series anomalies.

Dirichlet-multinomial: conjugate posterior over category probabilities. Core idea: Dirichlet prior Dir(α) on probability simplex; observe multinomial counts; posterior is Dir(α + counts). Sequential updates ≡ batch update (exchangeability). When to use: topic modeling, urn problems, belief updating on discrete distributions.

Empirical Bayes shrinkage (James-Stein style): shrink group means toward grand mean. Core idea: estimate hyperparameter from data; shrink group means via Bayesian posterior. Total squared error BEATS raw group means (Stein's paradox measured). When to use: meta-analysis, small-group inference, estimation of many parameters.

Gamma-Poisson conjugate prior: Gamma prior on Poisson rate parameter. Core idea: prior Gamma(α, β); observe Poisson counts; posterior is Gamma(α + Σcount, β + n). Sequential updates ≡ batch update (conjugacy). Posterior matches closed form. When to use: rate estimation, count data modeling, reliability/failure analysis.

Gaussian process regression (lite): RBF kernel, small n, direct Cholesky solve. Core idea: place Gaussian priors on function values; posterior mean interpolates training data. "Lite" = RBF kernel only, direct dense solve (no sparse/inducing points). When to use: small-data regression with uncertainty, interpolation, Bayesian optimization.

HMM Baum-Welch (EM) training: learn emission and transition probabilities. Core idea: E-step computes forward-backward statistics; M-step re-estimates parameters. Likelihood increases monotonically. Recovered probs ≈ planted truth. When to use: sequence tagging, time-series classification, learning from unlabeled sequences.

Particle filter (SMC): track a noisy 1D random walk target. Core idea: maintain weighted particles; predict, weight by observation likelihood, resample. Particle-mean RMSE beats raw observations; effective sample size monitors degeneracy. When to use: nonlinear filtering, state tracking, online Bayesian inference.

Rejection sampling: sample from complex density under an envelope. Core idea: sample from proposal, accept with probability p(x) / (M * q(x)). Empirical moments match numeric-integration moments; acceptance rate ≈ theoretical 1/M. When to use: non-standard distributions, Bayesian posterior sampling, missing primitives.

RTS (Rauch-Tung-Striebel) Kalman smoother: forward-backward pass for optimal smoothing. Core idea: forward Kalman filter, then backward pass corrects trajectory. Smoothed RMSE < filtered RMSE < raw observations. When to use: trajectory estimation, state inference after all data arrives.

Decision Tree Classifier using ID3 Algorithm (from scratch). Core idea: Recursively split data on the feature that gives the highest information gain (reduction in entropy). Build tree top-down, stopping when all samples are of one class or max depth is reached. When to use: Non-linear boundaries; interpretable rules; categorical/continuous data.

Gaussian Mixture Model (1D) via Expectation-Maximization (from scratch). Core idea: Model data as a mixture of k Gaussian distributions. EM iteratively infers cluster responsibilities (E-step) and updates Gaussian parameters (M-step). Converges to a local maximum of the likelihood. When to use: Soft clustering; probabilistic model of data; identifying mixture components.

k-Means Clustering (from scratch). Core idea: Partition data into k clusters by iteratively assigning samples to the nearest centroid and updating centroids to be the mean of assigned samples. Repeat until convergence (centroids stop moving). When to use: Unsupervised clustering; exploratory analysis; identifying natural groups.

k-Nearest Neighbors Classifier (from scratch). Core idea: To classify a new point, find the k nearest training samples using Euclidean distance and predict the majority class among them. No training phase; prediction is expensive but the model is simple and often effective. When to use: Non-linear boundaries; small to medium datasets; quick prototypes.

Linear Regression via Batch Gradient Descent (from scratch). Core idea: Given labeled training data (X, y), fit a linear model y = Xw + b by iteratively updating weights w and bias b to minimize mean squared error. Gradient descent computes ∂loss/∂w and ∂loss/∂b each iteration and moves opposite the gradient to reduce loss. When to use: Continuous target prediction; interpretable model; small to m

Binary Logistic Regression via Gradient Descent (from scratch). Core idea: Model binary classification via sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z). Given labeled data (X, y) where y ∈ {0, 1}, fit weights w and bias b by minimizing binary cross-entropy loss via gradient descent. When to use: Binary classification; interpretable probabilities; small to medium data.

Multinomial Naive Bayes for Text Classification (from scratch). Core idea: Represent documents as word-frequency vectors. Assume features (word counts) are conditionally independent given class. Compute P(class|doc) using Bayes' rule and word probabilities per class (with Laplace smoothing). When to use: Text classification (spam/ham, sentiment); fast training; baseline.

Principal Component Analysis via Power Iteration (from scratch). Core idea: Find directions of maximum variance in data by computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. Use power iteration to find the top eigenvector without full eigendecomposition. When to use: Dimensionality reduction; data visualization; noise reduction.

Perceptron Learning Algorithm (from scratch). Core idea: A linear classifier for linearly separable data. The perceptron iteratively updates weights on misclassified samples using the rule: w ← w + y_i * x_i for each error. Converges in finite steps on separable data. When to use: Binary classification on linearly separable data; fast training.

Ridge Regression via Normal Equations (from scratch). Core idea: Linear regression with L2 regularization: minimize ||Xw - y||^2 + λ||w||^2. Solved analytically via normal equations: w = (X^T X + λI)^(-1) X^T y. Implement matrix operations (transpose, multiply, Gaussian elimination) from scratch. When to use: Regression with collinearity; small to medium data; interpretable model.

Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC): rejection sampling for intractable likelihoods. Sample from prior, simulate data, accept if simulated ≈ observed (within ε). Core claim: posterior mean recovers the planted parameter; acceptance rate shrinks as ε tightens.

Bayes factor for comparing two normal means: H1 (θ ≠ 0) vs H0 (θ = 0). BF = p(data|H1) / p(data|H0). Core claim: BF>1 when H1 is true AND BF<1 when H0 is true (BOTH directions asserted; the two-sided test).

ELBO monotonicity in coordinate-ascent variational inference. Coordinate-ascent VI (CAVI) maximizes the Evidence Lower Bound one factor at a time; each update is a conditional maximizer, so the ELBO is NON-DECREASING every step, and it is bounded above by the true log-evidence (ELBO = log p(data) − KL(q‖posterior) ≤ log p(data)). For a conjugate Gaussian the bound is tight — CAVI converges to exac

Hierarchical shrinkage (James-Stein): partial-pooling beats no-pooling on MSE. When group means are estimated from noisy, small samples, shrinking them toward the grand mean reduces total error — the James-Stein effect. The positive-part JS estimator dominates the no-pooling (per-group MLE) estimator whenever there are ≥3 groups and sampling noise is non-trivial. Core claim: partial-pooling MSE-to

Laplace approximation: approximate posterior p(θ|data) with Gaussian at MAP. Curvature of the log-posterior at the mode provides variance. Core claim: Gaussian-at-MAP mode ≈ true MAP; curvature ≈ observed Fisher info.

Mean-field variational inference for a Gaussian with unknown mean AND precision. The true posterior over (μ, τ) is Normal-Gamma — NOT factorizable — so a mean-field q(μ)q(τ) is a genuine APPROXIMATION, not the analytic posterior in disguise. Coordinate- ascent VI (CAVI) iterates the two factors to convergence. Core claim: VI recovers the mean the data support (≈ sample mean ≈ true μ) and a positiv

Posterior contraction rate: posterior sd shrinks ~1/√n as sample size increases. Bayesian consistency: posterior concentrates on true parameter. Core claim: posterior sd shrinks ~1/√n as n grows (assert the ratio across two sample sizes).

Posterior predictive p-value: compare observed data to posterior predictive distribution. ppp ≈ 0.5 for the correct model; extreme (<0.05 or >0.95) for misspecified model. Core claim: ppp ≈ 0.5 for correct model; extreme for misspecified one.
R-hat convergence diagnostic: measures MCMC chain mixing. R̂ ≈ 1 for well-mixed chains, >1.1 for stuck chains. Core claim: R̂ ≈ 1 for well-mixed AND >1.1 for stuck (BOTH directions).

Simulation Based Calibration (SBC): ranks should be uniform for a well-calibrated sampler. Simulate parameter, simulate data, infer posterior, check where the true parameter ranks. Core claim: ranks ~uniform (χ²) for correct sampler; flagged non-uniform for biased one.

Cluster randomization: treatment assigned at the cluster level, not the individual. Intracluster correlation (ICC) means observations within a cluster are not independent, so the naive per-observation SE is too small — its 95% CIs UNDER-cover the true effect. Aggregating to cluster means and testing on those (n = #clusters) restores nominal coverage. Core claim: over many cluster-randomized datase

Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE): smallest effect size detectable with given n, α, power. Computed from normal approximation. Verified by simulation at multiple points. Core claim: MDE formula matches simulated power curve.

mSPRT (mixture Sequential Probability Ratio Test): an always-valid test. Under continuous peeking a fixed-α test inflates type-I badly. Holm correction (step-down Bonferroni) for multiple comparisons. Many variants of a treatment tested; uncorrected testing breaks FWER over replications. Holm correction controls FWER; trades power for false-positive control. Core claim: uncorrected breaks FWER; Holm holds it.

Network interference: SUTVA violation where spillover through a graph biases ATE. Treatment on one user affects neighbors (e.g., social network). Naive ATE (individual randomization) is biased due to spillover. Core claim: spillover biases naive ATE by measured amount; the classic trap, quantified.

Novelty effect: early treatment boost that fades over time. First measurement of a treatment shows inflated effect; long-run effect is lower. Core claim: day-1 estimate overstates long-run effect; time-sliced estimates reveal decay.

Peeking alpha inflation: continuous peeking at a fixed-n test inflates type-I error. Run test, peek at p-value, continue collecting if not significant, re-test. This inflates type-I from α=5% to ~20-30%. Core claim: peeking breaks type-I guarantee; measured over replications under null hypothesis.

Post-stratification variance reduction: stratify AFTER observing data, using prognostic covariate. On a prognostic covariate (correlated with outcome but NOT treated), stratifying reduces ATE estimator variance. Core claim: post-stratifying on prognostic covariate cuts variance by measured fraction vs simple difference-in-means.

Stratified randomization: randomize treatment within strata of a covariate. Better covariate balance + lower estimator variance vs simple randomization. Core claim: over seeded replications, stratified shows better balance and lower variance.

Switchback experiment: time-block randomization for marketplace interference. Under interference (treating some users spills over to controls), a user-split A/B is BIASED: the control arm is partially "treated" through the marketplace, so the measured treatment−control gap shrinks toward zero. Benford's law: leading digit distribution in many real datasets. P(digit d) = log₁₀(1 + 1/d) for d ∈ {1,...,9}. Multiplicative data follows; uniform data violates it. Chi-square test.
Birthday paradox: analytical vs simulated collision probability. P(≥2 same birthday in n people) ≈ 1 - n!/((365)^n · (365-n)!). Planted n values; analytic and simulated agree.

Gaussian copula: model dependence structure separately from marginals. Copula C(u, v) = P(U ≤ u, V ≤ v) where U, V ~ uniform; independence is C = uv. Core claim: rank correlation preserved under copula transform; planted copula recovered.
Coupon collector: expected trials to collect all n distinct items. E[T] = n·H_n where H_n = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n is harmonic series. Core claim: simulated mean matches n·H_n; planted n values.
Block maxima: fit Gumbel distribution to extreme values for return-level estimation. Core claim: planted return level recovered; CDF fit verified on known quantiles.
Inclusion-exclusion: count derangements (permutations with no fixed points). !n = n! · Σ (−1)^k / k! ≈ n! / e. Core claim: exact formula matches simulation; !n / n! → 1/e as n → ∞.

Pólya urn: reinforcement model whose limiting proportion is RANDOM ~ Beta(a, b). Start with a balls of color A, b of color B. Each draw: pick a ball, return it plus one more of the same color. The rich-get-richer feedback means a single urn's proportion does NOT converge to the mean a/(a+b) — it converges to a RANDOM limit distributed as Beta(a,b). Core claim (the actual theorem): across many urns

Quantile mapping: correct distributional bias by matching quantiles. Maps biased distribution onto reference via quantile alignment. Core claim: post-correction quantiles match reference; planted shift corrected.
Stirling's approximation: log(n!) ≈ n·log(n) - n + 0.5·log(2πn). Core claim: relative error shrinks as n grows; error measured vs exact factorial.

1D convolution layer learning to detect a planted motif in sequences. Core idea: Implement 1D convolution from scratch. Convolve a learnable kernel over a 1D sequence. Data contains a planted motif; over training the kernel learns to detect it, producing high responses when centered on the motif and low elsewhere. When to use: Understanding convolution mechanics, feature detection, temporal patter

Dropout regularization: network with vs without dropout on a noisy dataset. Core idea: Generate a small noisy dataset prone to overfitting. Train two networks: one with dropout (randomly zero hidden activations during training only) and one without. The dropout version regularizes the network and generalizes better to held-out validation data, especially on small datasets. When to use: Overfitting

Early stopping with patience-based validation monitoring. Core idea: Train a network and monitor validation loss each epoch. If validation loss doesn't improve for `patience` consecutive epochs, stop training early and restore the best weights seen. Prevents overfitting and wasted computation. When to use: Any supervised training with validation data, preventing overfitting, efficient hyperparamet

Learning rate schedules: constant vs step-decay vs cosine annealing. Core idea: Train the same network three times with different LR schedules on the same problem. Show that step-decay and cosine schedules reach comparable or better final loss with more stable late-phase updates compared to constant high LR. When to use: Hyperparameter tuning, convergence acceleration, avoiding divergence in late

2-Layer MLP trained by hand-derived backpropagation on XOR. Core idea: Manually implement the forward pass (linear -> sigmoid), backward pass (chain rule through sigmoid), and weight updates. Learn to solve XOR by driving loss to near zero. When to use: Understanding backpropagation mechanics, debugging autodiff systems, verifying network training fundamentals.

Verify analytic backprop gradients against finite-difference numerical gradients. Core idea: Compute gradients both ways (backprop and numerical finite-difference) on the same tiny network. Compare element-wise; if max relative error < 1e-4, backprop is correct. Essential debugging pattern for any hand-rolled network. When to use: Verifying custom backprop implementations, debugging gradient bugs,

Multi-class softmax regression with cross-entropy loss. Core idea: Learn to classify 3 synthetic clusters in 2D using a linear classifier with softmax output and cross-entropy loss. Gradient descent updates weights to maximize log-probability of true class. When to use: Multiclass classification, understanding softmax and cross-entropy, baseline for any categorical prediction task.

1-hidden-layer autoencoder compressing correlated 8D data to 2D and back. Core idea: Encoder maps 8D input -> 2D bottleneck via sigmoid. Decoder maps 2D -> 8D reconstruction. Train to minimize reconstruction error. With correlated input (columns highly linearly dependent), 2D bottleneck should capture main variance; reconstruction error should be far below random baseline. When to use: Dimensional

Weight initialization comparison: naive vs Xavier/He initialization. Core idea: Build a deeper network (5 layers) and train it with three different initialization schemes: (1) small random [-0.1, 0.1], (2) large random [-1, 1], (3) Xavier initialization (std proportional to 1/sqrt(fan_in)).
