Skip-gram word2vec with negative sampling on a tiny built-in corpus. Core idea: For each target word, predict context words using a learnable embedding matrix. Use negative sampling: update embeddings to score true context pairs high and random (context, negative-word) pairs low. Related words (co-occurring in context) converge to nearby embeddings. When to use: Word embeddings, unsupervised seman

Graham scan: compute convex hull of a point set. Core idea: sort points by polar angle from lowest point, use stack to maintain left-turn invariant. Hull vertices are exactly the extremes. When to use: bounding envelopes, distance metrics, collision bounds.

Douglas-Peucker polyline simplification: reduce point count while bounding deviation. Core idea: find point with max distance to chord; if > epsilon, recurse on both halves; otherwise remove all intermediate points. Output ⊂ input, max deviation ≤ epsilon. When to use: map rendering, trajectory compression, lossy path storage.

Geohash: encode/decode lat/lon as interleaved bit string, base-32 encoded. Core idea: recursively bisect latitude and longitude, interleave bits, encode as base32. Neighbors share prefixes; precision ∝ string length. When to use: spatial indexing, proximity queries, tile-based mapping.

Great-circle intermediate waypoints via spherical linear interpolation (slerp). Core idea: interpolate along great circle arc between two points on Earth sphere. Verify each waypoint's cumulative distance equals proportional share of total distance. When to use: flight path generation, mapping geodetic routes, animation along globe.

2D grid density binning: partition points into cells, count per-cell density. Core idea: divide (minx,miny)-(maxx,maxy) into regular grid; assign points to cells; count occupancy. Planted hotspot lands in correct cell; total count = input count. When to use: heatmaps, spatial statistics, clustering pre-processing.

Haversine great-circle distance and initial bearing. Core idea: compute geodetic distance between lat/lon points on Earth sphere, and the initial compass bearing from first to second point. When to use: routing, distance matrices on geographic coordinates.

Ray casting algorithm: test if a point is inside a polygon. Core idea: cast a ray from point to infinity; count edge crossings. Odd count = inside, even = outside. Handles concave and convex polygons. When to use: geofencing, collision detection, geographic containment.

Shoelace formula: polygon area and centroid from vertex coordinates. Core idea: area via sum of cross products; centroid via weighted average. Works for both convex and concave polygons (signed area can be negative). When to use: geometry calculations, shape analysis, mass properties.

Quadtree: spatial indexing for range queries on 2D point sets. Core idea: recursively subdivide space into 4 quadrants; insert points; range query recursively searches overlapping cells, much fewer distance checks than brute force on large sets. When to use: spatial search, collision detection, visibility culling.

Radius join via grid bucketing: find all points-within-radius-of-centers pairs. Core idea: grid bucket points and centers; for each center, check points in nearby cells only. Equals brute force result but with far fewer distance checks on dense point sets. When to use: spatial clustering, nearest-neighbor search, network analysis.

Cohort retention analysis from event logs. Group users by cohort (e.g., signup month/cohort), track which cohorts return in subsequent periods, and compute retention curves. Identifies which cohorts have better/worse long-term engagement. Use: subscription/SaaS analytics, user lifecycle analysis, retention funnels.

Cross-validation data leakage from preprocessing before splitting. Feature selection fit on the FULL dataset before train-test split leaks information from test into train, inflating CV scores. Correct approach: fit feature selection inside each fold on training data only. Use: detecting CV score inflation, validating proper cross-validation pipelines.

Population Stability Index (PSI) and KS-statistic for feature drift detection. PSI measures how a feature's distribution shifts between a reference period (e.g., training data) and a current window (e.g., production data). KS-statistic tests whether two distributions are significantly different. Both detect dataset shift / concept drift. Use: production monitoring, model retraining triggers, data

Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) for streaming metrics. EWMA smooths noisy streaming data while reacting quickly to level shifts. Each new observation is weighted inversely to its age (older = lower weight). More responsive than simple moving average, smoother than raw values. Use: real-time monitoring, anomaly detection, adaptive thresholds.

Feature hashing for dimensionality reduction of high-dimensional sparse features. Hash trick maps unbounded categorical/text features to a fixed number of dimensions via hashing. Trade-off: reduces memory/computation but introduces collisions. Deterministic, works online, and maintains separability for classification tasks. Use: text/NLP feature extraction, streaming data, memory-constrained setti

Multi-step funnel conversion analysis with confidence intervals. Track user progression through a conversion funnel (e.g., visit → signup → purchase → retain). Compute step-wise conversion rates with Wilson confidence intervals. Identify the weakest step. Use: product analytics, sales/marketing funnels, conversion rate optimization.

RFM customer segmentation: Recency, Frequency, Monetary. Segment customers based on: - Recency: days since last purchase - Frequency: number of purchases - Monetary: total spend RFM scores divide each metric into quartiles, then combine into segments (e.g., "whale" = high on all three, "churned" = low on all). Use: customer value analysis, retention targeting, marketing segmentation.

Simpson's Paradox: aggregate trend reverses within strata. An association between two variables at the aggregate level reverses direction when data is split by a confounding variable (stratum). Classic example: treatment A beats B overall, but B beats A within every subgroup. Use: causal inference, detecting confounding, interpreting correlations.

Target encoding with smoothing + out-of-fold fitting. Target (mean) encoding replaces a category with the mean target of that category — powerful, and the classic way to leak: if the encoding is fit on data that includes the rows being encoded (or the test set), the feature memorizes target noise and shows FAKE predictive skill. Two defenses, both implemented here: SMOOTHING (shrink rare-category

Welford's online algorithm for running mean and variance. Welford's algorithm computes running mean and variance in a single pass with O(1) memory and perfect numerical stability. It avoids the naive sum-of-squares formula which catastrophically cancels when data has a large offset. Use: streaming metrics, online parameter updates, memory-constrained environments.

Covariance Matrix Pattern. Computes sample covariance between all numeric columns. Core idea: covariance measures how two variables jointly vary (sign = direction of relationship, magnitude = strength). Diagonal contains variance of each variable. When to use: understanding variance structure, multivariate analysis, principal component analysis setup, detecting correlations with magnitude awarenes

Data Profiling Summary Pattern. Per-column profile of a mixed dataset (numeric/categorical): type inference, missing count, cardinality, min/max/mean for numeric, top values for categorical. Core idea: one-pass summary to understand data structure, missingness, range, and uniqueness without external libraries. When to use: exploratory data analysis, data quality checks, understanding dataset struc

Histogram Builder Pattern. Constructs a histogram using equal-width bins with automatic bin-count selection (Sturges' rule). Core idea: Sturges rule k = ceil(log2(n) + 1) works well for normal data; easy rule without parameter tuning. When to use: exploratory data analysis, visualizing distributions, detecting multimodality, choosing reasonable bin counts automatically.

Missing Value Imputation Pattern. Replaces None/NaN values with statistical estimates (mean, median, mode) or creates binary missing-indicator columns. Core idea: preserve sample count while reconstructing plausible values from complete records; track missingness separately. When to use: handling incomplete datasets before analysis, preserving row count, understanding missing-data patterns, tree-b

One-Hot Encoding Pattern. Converts categorical features into binary indicators (one-hot vectors). Core idea: represent each unique category value with a binary column per category, exactly one column = 1, rest = 0. Essential for feeding categorical data to algorithms that expect numeric input. When to use: preprocessing categorical columns before model training, feature engineering for tree-free a

Pearson Correlation Matrix Pattern. Computes pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients between all numeric columns from scratch. Core idea: measure linear association; correlation is covariance normalized by standard deviations. Symmetric matrix with 1s on diagonal. When to use: exploratory data analysis to identify relationships, feature selection (drop highly correlated features), multicollinear

Quantile Binning Pattern. Partitions a continuous numeric column into equal-frequency bins (quantile-based) vs equal-width bins. Core idea: quantile binning preserves bin counts (roughly equal) even on skewed data; equal-width creates imbalanced bins on skew. When to use: discretizing continuous features, handling skewed distributions, creating balanced categorical features, non-uniform binning.

Random Oversampling and Synthetic Minority Balance Pattern. Rebalances imbalanced datasets by random oversampling (duplicate minority) and SMOTE-lite (interpolate between minority neighbors). Core idea: majority class stays fixed, minority class is augmented to match majority size via repetition and interpolation. When to use: imbalanced classification, oversampling minority before training, creat

Three-Way Stratified Split Pattern. Partitions a dataset into train/validation/test sets while preserving class proportions in all three splits. Core idea: stratification ensures each split is representative of the full distribution (important for imbalanced data). When to use: classification datasets, ensuring all class proportions preserved, train-val-test evaluation protocols, handling imbalanc

Winsorization and Clipping Pattern. Caps extreme values at percentile thresholds (winsorization) or hard bounds (clipping). Core idea: reduce influence of outliers while preserving sample count and general structure; interior values untouched. When to use: outlier mitigation before analysis, handling measurement errors, reducing leverage of extreme observations, robust preprocessing.

Team-Draft Interleaving for A/B Testing Rankers. Compare two rankers (A and B) by interleaving their results in a single ranking. Users click on interleaved results. The ranker whose document the user clicked on wins that "team". We count wins and determine which ranker is better. We plant a stronger ranker and verify it wins the interleaving.

BM25 Ranking (Okapi BM25). BM25 ranks documents by relevance to a query via TF-IDF with saturation and length normalization. BM25 outperforms raw TF on length-biased corpora (long docs get unfair boost without normalization). We plant a query, make one doc longer (same term frequency but inflated raw TF), verify BM25 ranks the relevant doc higher despite length bias while naive TF is confused by l

Elo Rating System. Maintain skill ratings via pairwise wins/losses. Elo(new) = Elo(old) + K * (observed - expected). Expected score = 1 / (1 + 10^((opponent_elo - my_elo)/400)). We plant a stronger player and verify their Elo converges higher; hand-verify the expected-score formula against observed win rate.

Inverted Index and Boolean Search. Build an inverted index (term → docs), then answer AND/OR queries. We verify that planted relevant docs are retrieved, irrelevant excluded, and set operations match hand-computed results.

Ranking metrics suite: Mean Reciprocal Rank, Precision@K, Recall@K. MRR = mean over queries of 1/(rank of the first relevant item). Precision@K = |relevant ∩ top-K| / K. Recall@K = |relevant ∩ top-K| / |relevant|. Core claim: each metric returns its EXACT known value on a planted ranking, and MRR falls monotonically as the first relevant item is demoted.

NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain). Evaluate ranking quality: DCG sums relevance scores discounted by position. NDCG normalizes DCG by ideal DCG (perfect ranking). Perfect ranking = NDCG 1.0, shuffled = lower score. We verify on a hand-computed example and show degraded ranking scores lower.

Pairwise Ranking via Logistic Regression. Learn item ordering from pairwise comparisons: for each pair (i,j), fit logistic regression on feature difference (f_i - f_j) to predict which ranks higher. Verify on planted item order: learned model should recover the order with high Kendall tau correlation vs truth.

Position Bias in Click Models and Inverse Propensity Weighting. Users click documents based on both relevance and position (position bias). Naive click-count ranking is confounded by position. Inverse propensity weighting (IPW) corrects for position bias; we verify that IPW recovers the true relevance order while naive click-count does not.

Pseudo-Relevance Feedback (PRF) for Query Expansion. Expand a query with terms from top-k initially-retrieved docs. PRF finds synonym/related-term docs that the raw query misses. We plant docs with synonyms, show that raw query misses them but expanded query finds them.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Combine multiple rankers via RRF: score = Σ (1 / (k + rank_i)). Fusion often beats individual rankers on noisy signals. We plant two mediocre rankers and show that fusing them recovers better ranking.

DISTANCE METRICS: Euclidean, Manhattan, Minkowski, Chebyshev, Cosine Core idea: Unified toolkit for common distance metrics on vectors. Each metric emphasizes different aspects: Euclidean (straight-line), Manhattan (grid), Chebyshev (max-coordinate), Minkowski (parametric generalization), Cosine (angle). When to use: KNN, clustering, anomaly detection, or any task requiring multi-purpose distance

DISTANCE METRIC: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) Core idea: Align two time series by warping time, allowing elastic matching of temporal patterns. DTW distance <= euclidean distance and captures shape similarity better than point-wise metrics. Includes optimal alignment path reconstruction. When to use: Time series comparison, speech recognition, gesture recognition, or any domain where temporal stretc

OPTIMIZATION: Epsilon-Greedy Multi-Armed Bandit Core idea: In a multi-armed bandit, each arm yields stochastic reward. Epsilon-greedy balances exploration (try random arms) vs exploitation (pull best known). Pure greedy exploits only; epsilon-greedy explores with probability epsilon. When to use: Online decision-making with unknown reward distributions (ad serving, clinical trials, A/B testing). E

FEATURE SCALING: Min-Max, Z-Score, Robust Scaling Core idea: Different scaling methods normalize features to comparable ranges. Min-max scales to [0, 1]; z-score centers to mean=0, std=1; robust uses median/IQR to resist outliers. Choose based on data distribution and algorithm requirements. When to use: KNN, SVM, neural networks, or any algorithm sensitive to feature magnitude. Verify output prop

OPTIMIZATION: Genetic Algorithm (Selection, Crossover, Mutation) Core idea: Population-based metaheuristic mimicking natural evolution. Iteratively select fit individuals, combine (crossover), mutate, and replace to explore the solution space. Demonstrates OneMax (all bits to 1) and a deceptive variant. When to use: Combinatorial optimization, non-differentiable landscapes, or when exploring diver

OPTIMIZATION: Gradient Descent with Momentum Core idea: Vanilla gradient descent oscillates in narrow valleys; momentum accumulates velocity across iterations, smoothing the path and converging faster. Compare vanilla GD vs momentum GD on a 2D quadratic bowl. When to use: Convex optimization with non-isotropic (elongated) loss landscapes; standard in neural network training to accelerate convergen

OPTIMIZATION: Hill Climbing with Random Restarts Core idea: Pure hill climbing gets stuck in local optima on rugged landscapes. Random restarts re-initialize from different points and return the best result found across all restarts, allowing escape from local optima. When to use: Local search on landscapes with many local optima; simple, fast, and effective when computational budget allows multip

DISTANCE METRIC: Mahalanobis Distance Core idea: Euclidean distance treats all dimensions equally; Mahalanobis accounts for covariance structure, scaling by the inverse covariance matrix. On correlated data, Mahalanobis distance can reveal structure that Euclidean misses. When to use: Multivariate outlier detection, anomaly detection on correlated data, or whenever covariance structure is meaningf

OPTIMIZATION: Newton's Method for 1D Minimization Core idea: Use second-order (curvature) information via the Hessian to take smarter steps than gradient descent. Newton's method quadratically converges near the optimum, often faster than first-order methods on well-conditioned problems. When to use: 1D or small-scale smooth optimization where second derivatives are available; faster convergence t

OPTIMIZATION: Simulated Annealing Core idea: Mimic metallic annealing by accepting worse solutions with decreasing probability as "temperature" cools. Escapes local optima by allowing uphill moves early, becoming greedy as temperature drops. When to use: Non-convex, multi-modal functions where gradient-based methods fail; combinatorial optimization (TSP, scheduling) and black-box function minimiza

Expectation-Maximization (EM) Algorithm: Two-Coin Problem. Estimates two coin biases from mixed flip sessions without labels. The classic EM example: data is ambiguous (which coin produced each session?). Use when data is incomplete or missing labels for mixture components.

Gibbs Sampling for Bivariate Normal Distribution. Alternately samples each variable from its conditional distribution. Recovers correlation structure from a correlated bivariate normal. Use when joint sampling is hard but conditionals are tractable.

Importance Sampling for Expectation Estimation. Estimates E_target[h(X)] using samples from a proposal, re-weighted by the ratio. Useful when the target is hard to sample but easy to evaluate. Use when direct sampling is infeasible but density ratio is computable.

Kaplan-Meier Survival Curve with Censored Observations. Estimates a survival function from time-to-event data with right censoring. Computes the product of (1 - events/at_risk) at each event time. Use when analyzing time-to-event data with censoring (medical, reliability, churn).

Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) with Gaussian Kernel & Silverman Bandwidth. Non-parametric density estimation via kernel smoothing. Bandwidth chosen by Silverman's rule: h = (4/(3*n))^(1/5) * sigma. Use for smooth density estimates from raw samples.

LOESS-Lite: Locally Weighted Linear Regression. Fits a piecewise linear regression using tricube-weighted local neighborhoods. Simple non-parametric smoothing for noisy signals. Use for smooth, adaptive curve fitting without assuming global model form.

Metropolis-Hastings MCMC Sampling. Samples from a target distribution using a random-walk proposal. Accepts/rejects proposals based on the Metropolis-Hastings ratio. Use when you need posterior samples from a complex distribution.

Polynomial Regression via Least Squares (Vandermonde Design Matrix). A polynomial regression solver using Gaussian elimination on the Vandermonde matrix. Fits a degree-d polynomial to (x, y) data by solving the normal equations directly. Use when you need interpretable polynomial fit without external libraries.

Power Analysis: Sample Size for Two-Proportion Z-Test. Computes required sample size per group for a given effect size, alpha, and power using normal approximation. Verifies the computed n reproduces the target power. Use for study design when comparing two proportions.

Quantile Regression via Pinball Loss and Gradient Descent. Estimates conditional quantiles (e.g., median, 90th percentile) by minimizing the pinball (check) loss: L_tau(y, pred) = (tau - 1)*min(y-pred,0) + tau*max(y-pred,0). Use when you need robust estimates of specific quantiles instead of the mean.

Autocorrelation Function (ACF) Compute the autocorrelation of a time series at multiple lags. ACF(k) = correlation between y_t and y_{t-k}. Include simple significance bounds (±2/sqrt(n)) to identify significant lags. Use to detect seasonality and memory in the data.

Autoregressive (AR) Model Fit an AR(p) model by regressing y_t on its p lagged values using least squares. Solves the normal equations directly (no external libraries). Produces one-step-ahead forecasts. Use for univariate time series prediction when past values predict the future.

CUSUM Change-Point Detection Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) control chart detects shifts in mean. CUSUM_t = max(0, CUSUM_{t-1} + (y_t - target) - k) When CUSUM exceeds a threshold h, a change is signaled. Use to detect step changes in level (e.g., sensor drift, process shift).

Differencing for Stationarity First differencing transforms a non-stationary series (e.g., random walk) into a stationary one. Differenced series: d_t = y_t - y_{t-1}. Stationarity (constant mean, variance) enables forecasting with AR models. Demonstrate that differencing reduces mean and variance drift in a trend.

Exponential Smoothing Apply single exponential smoothing (Simple Exponential Smoothing, SES) and double exponential smoothing (Holt's method) to a time series. SES smooths level; Holt's also captures linear trend. Use for short-horizon forecasting when trend matters (e.g., demand planning).

1D Kalman Filter Recursively estimate the state of a 1D system (constant velocity model). State: x = [position, velocity]. Observations are noisy position measurements. The filter balances prediction (prior) and observation (likelihood) using Gaussian uncertainties (variances). Reduces observation noise. Use for smoothing GPS, sensor readings, or tracking slow-moving targets.

Moving Average Smoothing Smooth a noisy time series using simple and weighted moving averages. Reduces short-term fluctuations while preserving trend; wider windows smooth more but lag the signal. Use for noise reduction in raw sensor or market data.

Rolling Z-Score Anomaly Detection Detect anomalies using rolling-window z-scores. For each point, compute the z-score within a rolling window: z = (x - window_mean) / window_std. Flag points where |z| exceeds a threshold (e.g., 3) as anomalies. Use for detecting sudden spikes or drops in streaming data.

Seasonal Decomposition (Naive Additive) Decompose a time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components using naive additive decomposition: y_t = trend_t + seasonal_t + residual_t. Trend extracted via centered moving average; seasonal via period-wise means. Use to understand and remove seasonal patterns from data.

Walk-Forward Validation Time-series cross-validation using expanding windows: train on the first window, forecast 1 step ahead, expand window by 1, repeat. Evaluates forecasters on realistic out-of-sample data without lookahead bias. Compare multiple forecasters (naive mean vs. other methods) using MAE.

Apriori algorithm for frequent itemsets and association rules. Core idea: iteratively find frequent itemsets by checking support thresholds, then generate association rules with confidence and lift metrics. When to use: when you have a transaction database and want to discover patterns like "customers who buy X also buy Y" (market-basket analysis).

Bayesian A/B testing with Beta-Binomial posteriors. Core idea: model each variant's success rate as Beta distribution, update posterior with observed data (successes + failures), then estimate P(B > A) via posterior sampling. When to use: when you want a probabilistic answer to "is B better than A?" with uncertainty quantification, especially for small sample sizes.

IQR-based outlier detection. Core idea: compute the interquartile range (Q3 - Q1), then flag any value outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR] as an outlier. When to use: for univariate outlier detection in numeric data, especially when you want a simple, interpretable method.

Item-based collaborative filtering. Core idea: compute adjusted-cosine similarity between item rating vectors (normalize by subtracting per-user mean), then recommend top-k unseen items using weighted similarity to items the user has already rated. When to use: when items have similar rating patterns across users and you want item-stability (item similarities change less frequently than user simil

Matrix factorization via stochastic gradient descent. Core idea: decompose a sparse rating matrix into user (U) and item (V) factor matrices of low rank, trained by SGD to minimize rating prediction error. Convergence is verified by RMSE dropping below a threshold. When to use: when you have sparse user-item rating data and want latent factors for dimensionality reduction or to fill missing entrie

Monte Carlo estimation: pi and definite integrals. Core idea: estimate quantities via random sampling. For pi: sample points in a unit square, count those inside the inscribed circle. For integrals: sample from the domain and average the function values, scaled by volume. When to use: for estimating integrals or geometric quantities where direct computation is hard; error shrinks as O(1/sqrt(n)).

Mutual information for feature selection. Core idea: compute entropy and mutual information between discrete features and a label, then rank features by MI. Informative features have higher MI than noise. When to use: for feature importance ranking in classification or regression, especially with discrete/categorical data.

PageRank via power iteration. Core idea: iterate score propagation through a directed graph where each node distributes its score equally to outgoing neighbors, with damping (teleport probability) to handle dangling nodes. Convergence is tested. When to use: when you need to rank nodes in a directed graph by importance (e.g., web pages, citations, social networks).

Thompson sampling for multi-armed bandits. Core idea: maintain Beta posteriors over success probability for each arm, sample from each posterior, pull the arm with highest sample, update via Bayesian update. Balances exploration vs exploitation optimally. When to use: when you need to allocate resources (A/B test, optimization) and want to minimize regret by learning arm quality online.

User-based collaborative filtering. Core idea: compute cosine similarity between user rating vectors, then predict ratings for unseen items as a weighted average of similar users' ratings. When to use: when you have user×item rating data and want to leverage user similarities to make personalized recommendations.

Bag-of-Words Vectorizer Core idea: represent each document as a sparse count vector of word frequencies. Build a shared vocabulary from all documents, then encode each document as counts over that vocabulary. Useful for baseline text representation before more complex methods. Use when: you need a simple baseline text representation, want to measure document similarity by raw term overlap, or need

Simplified Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) Tokenizer Core idea: learn merge operations from a corpus (combining frequent character pairs), then apply merges to tokenize new text. Encode text to token IDs, decode back to text. Use when: understanding subword tokenization, building custom tokenizers for small models, or studying how BPE reduces vocabulary size.

Cosine Similarity Search: Rank Documents by Query Core idea: convert documents and query to TF-IDF vectors, rank documents by cosine similarity to query. Fast baseline for relevance ranking and information retrieval. Use when: building a search engine, ranking results by relevance, finding top-k similar documents without heavy infrastructure.

Levenshtein Edit Distance via Dynamic Programming Core idea: compute minimum number of single-character edits (insert, delete, replace) to transform one string into another using DP. Backtrace the DP table to recover the actual edit sequence. Use when: measuring string similarity (spelling correction, fuzzy matching), finding near-duplicate text, or aligning sequences for comparison.

Word-Level Markov Chain Text Generator Core idea: build a transition matrix of word frequencies (conditional on previous word). Generate text by sampling from this distribution at each step, deterministic given seed. Useful for understanding Markov assumptions, text generation baselines, and data exploration. Use when: generating synthetic text, understanding term co-occurrence, building simple la

MinHash Signatures for Near-Duplicate Detection Core idea: compute compact hash signatures for sets of tokens. Use Jaccard similarity from signatures to estimate similarity and detect near-duplicates. Verify against exact Jaccard computation. Use when: detecting similar documents, deduplicating text corpora, or building scalable similarity search without comparing all pairs directly.

N-gram Language Model with Add-One Smoothing Core idea: model text as a Markov chain over n-grams (sequences of n tokens). Estimate P(token | preceding n-1 tokens) from data; use add-one smoothing to handle unseen contexts. Measure quality via perplexity on held-out text. Use when: generating text, evaluating text likelihood, building simple language models without neural networks, or studying Mar

RAKE-Style Keyword Extraction Core idea: split text into phrases delimited by stopwords, score phrases by degree (unique words in phrase) and frequency (how often phrase appears). Higher-scoring phrases are likely meaningful keywords. Use when: extracting keywords from documents, summarizing text topics, building terminology indices, or understanding key concepts in unstructured text.

TF-IDF Vectorizer Core idea: weight term frequencies by inverse document frequency to emphasize distinctive terms. TF-IDF(t,d) = freq(t in d) * log(N / doc_count(t)). Common baseline for document ranking and similarity. Use when: ranking documents by relevance to a query, finding similar documents, or preparing text for ML classifiers where term importance matters.

Viterbi Decoding for Hidden Markov Models Core idea: find the most-likely sequence of hidden states given observations using dynamic programming. Compare Viterbi result against brute-force enumeration to verify correctness. Use when: POS tagging, named entity recognition, sequence labeling problems, or understanding the Viterbi algorithm on toy examples.

AdaBoost Classification with Decision Stumps. AdaBoost sequentially fits weak learners (decision stumps) by reweighting training examples: samples misclassified by the current stump get higher weight in the next round. The ensemble combines weak learners with weights based on their accuracy. Use when: iterative ensemble for classification, balancing examples hard to classify.

Bagging for Variance Reduction. Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains many copies of an UNSTABLE base learner on bootstrap resamples and averages them. The averaged predictor has markedly lower variance across retrainings than a single base learner — that reduction, measured at fixed test points over many independent training draws, is the whole point of the method. (A stable learner like plain l

Gradient Boosting with Decision Stumps. Gradient boosting iteratively fits weak learners (depth-1 decision trees) to residuals of the previous ensemble, with each new tree weighted by a learning rate. Training loss decreases monotonically and the ensemble beats a single stump on regression. Use when: sequential ensemble improvement, regression on tabular data.

Huber Loss Robust Regression. Huber loss is a hybrid of squared loss (for small residuals) and absolute loss (for large residuals). It reduces sensitivity to outliers compared to OLS while staying smooth. Coefficients estimated under Huber loss are closer to ground truth under heavy-tailed noise. Use when: data with heavy-tailed noise, outlier robustness, smooth gradients.

Random Forest Classification. Random forest builds multiple decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample of the data and with random feature subsets at each split. The ensemble averages predictions across trees, reducing overfitting variance. Use when: robust classification on noisy data, feature importance, parallel training.

RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus) for Robust Regression. RANSAC iteratively selects random minimal subsets of data, fits models, and counts inliers (points close to the model). The model with the most inliers is returned, robustly ignoring gross outliers. Use when: data with severe outliers, unknown noise distribution, automatic outlier detection.

Spectral Clustering Lite. Spectral clustering constructs a graph Laplacian from pairwise affinities, computes its eigenvector (via power iteration), and clusters by the sign of the Fiedler vector. It recovers non-convex clusters (e.g., two moons) where k-means fails. Use when: non-convex cluster shapes, graph-based clustering, manifold structure.

Stacking Ensemble with Meta-Learner. Stacking trains a meta-learner on predictions from base models trained via out-of-fold cross-validation. The meta-learner learns to combine the base models' strengths, often outperforming the base models individually. Use when: combining diverse base models, high-dimensional feature space, complex patterns.

Theil-Sen Median-of-Slopes Estimator. Theil-Sen fits a line by computing slopes between all pairs of points and taking the median slope (robust to outliers). The intercept is the median of residuals after subtracting the slope. This non-parametric method is more robust than OLS under outliers. Use when: non-parametric robust regression, known outliers, distribution-free estimation.

Voting Classifier with Multiple Weak Learners. Voting combines predictions from multiple different base classifiers using hard voting (majority vote) or soft voting (average probabilities). The ensemble's accuracy typically exceeds the average individual accuracy. Use when: combining diverse classifiers, leveraging different model strengths.

Conjugate gradient: iterative solver for symmetric positive-definite systems. Solves A·x = b using search directions conjugate w.r.t. A. Core claim: converges in at most n iterations (vs potentially n iterations for Gaussian elimination), exact arithmetic. Planted SPD system; convergence verified, solution accuracy checked.

Gauss–Seidel vs Jacobi: convergence rate comparison. Both are stationary iterative solvers for A·x = b. Gauss–Seidel uses updated values immediately; Jacobi uses old values. Core claim: Gauss–Seidel converges faster (lower spectral radius). Planted system; iteration counts measured, ratio verified (typically 2–5x faster).

Householder reflection: zeros out components via hyperplane reflection. Given vector x, finds reflection matrix H = I - 2·v·v^T that maps x to [||x||, 0, 0, ...]. Used in QR, eigenvalue, and least-squares algorithms. Core claim: reflection computed; planted vector mapped to scaled unit vector.

Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm: iterative diagonalization of symmetric matrix. Applies Givens rotations to progressively zero off-diagonal elements. Core claim: converges to diagonal matrix of eigenvalues; eigenvectors are product of rotations. Planted 3×3 symmetric matrix; eigenvalues verified vs characteristic polynomial roots.

Least-squares via QR: solve A·x ≈ b using numerically stable QR factorization. QR decomposes A into orthogonal Q and upper-triangular R. Then A·x = b becomes R·x = Q^T·b (small overdetermined system). Numerically more stable than normal equations A^T·A·x = A^T·b. Core claim: solution recovered with better conditioning. Planted overdetermined system; solution accuracy vs normal equations compared.

LU decomposition with partial pivoting: PA = LU factorization. Permutation matrix P reorders rows for numerical stability; L and U satisfy PA = LU. Core claim: factorization recovered exactly; reconstruction PA = LU verified. Planted 3×3 matrix; decomposition and forward/backward solves tested.

Matrix condition number: measure sensitivity to perturbations in A and b. κ(A) = ||A|| · ||A⁻¹||. Large κ means small changes in A or b cause large changes in solution x. Core claim: error amplification measured; ill-conditioned system shows large error magnification vs small-κ system, identical perturbation size.

Power iteration with shift: find smallest eigenvalue via (A - σI) iteration. Power iteration on A finds largest |λ|. Shifting by σ gives largest |λ - σ|, which is the smallest eigenvalue if σ > largest eigenvalue. Core claim: smallest eigenvalue recovered; shift verified optimal. Planted symmetric matrix; smallest eigenvalue vs Jacobi diagonalization checked.

QR decomposition via Gram–Schmidt: orthogonal Q and upper-triangular R. Iteratively orthogonalizes columns of A to produce Q. Core claim: Q is orthonormal (Q^T·Q = I), A = Q·R verified. Planted 3×3 matrix; orthonormality and reconstruction tested.

Woodbury matrix identity: update A⁻¹ efficiently after rank-1 A change. If A_new = A + u·v^T, then (A_new)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ - (A⁻¹·u·v^T·A⁻¹) / (1 + v^T·A⁻¹·u). Core claim: inverse updated in O(n²) vs O(n³) re-inversion. Planted rank-1 update; updated inverse verified exactly against full recomputation.

Class Weights for Imbalanced Classification Core idea: When classes are imbalanced (e.g., 95% negative, 5% positive), training loss can favor predicting the majority class. Assigning higher weight to the minority class penalizes misclassification more, recovering minority recall. When to use: Binary or multiclass classification with severe class imbalance, where you care about minority class perfo

Split-Conformal Prediction Intervals for Regression Core idea: Split data into train/calibration. Train a regression model, then on calibration data compute residuals to set interval width such that coverage is guaranteed. When to use: You want prediction intervals with a formal coverage guarantee, even if the model is miscalibrated or the error distribution is non-Gaussian.

Grid Search vs Random Search: Demonstrating Random Search Efficiency Core idea: When hyperparameter space is high-dimensional but only a few params matter, random search explores more efficiently than grid search. When to use: You have many hyperparams but limited evaluation budget, or want to understand when random search is preferable to grid search.

Model Persistence Roundtrip (Save and Reload) Core idea: Train a model, serialize it to JSON, reload it, and verify predictions are identical (bit-for-bit for floats, or within machine epsilon). When to use: You need to confirm that model serialization/deserialization preserves all parameters and produces deterministic predictions on new data.

Partial Dependence Plot (PD) — Data Generation Core idea: For each feature, marginalize over other features and plot the average model prediction as that feature varies. Linear features show monotone curves; noise features show flat. When to use: You want to understand the marginal effect of a feature on predictions, holding other features constant in aggregate.

Permutation Feature Importance Core idea: Shuffle each feature independently on held-out data and measure the drop in model performance. Features whose shuffling hurts performance are important; noise features don't affect predictions when shuffled. When to use: You've trained a model and want to rank features by their predictive contribution, agnostic to the model's internal structure.

Platt Scaling for Probability Calibration Core idea: When a classifier outputs uncalibrated scores (overconfident), fit a logistic function (Platt scaling) on a hold-out set to map scores to true probabilities. When to use: You've trained a classifier and want to recalibrate its confidence scores to match true conditional probabilities, improving Brier score and reliability diagrams.

Shapley Value Sampling (Monte Carlo Approximation) Core idea: Estimate each feature's marginal contribution via random coalition sampling. For a simple additive model, sampled Shapley values should match analytic per-feature contributions. When to use: You want fair feature attribution that respects coalition marginal values, without computing all 2^n coalitions exactly.

Successive Halving for Hyperparameter Optimization Core idea: Allocate more resources to promising configurations, halving the pool at each stage. Early elimination of poor performers saves budget while identifying good configs. When to use: You have many hyperparameter candidates but limited evaluation budget, and want to concentrate resources on the most promising ones.

Threshold Tuning with Asymmetric Misclassification Costs Core idea: Binary classifiers typically use 0.5 threshold, but with asymmetric costs (e.g., false negatives cost more than false positives), the optimal threshold shifts. When to use: Fraud detection (missing fraud = high cost) or spam filtering (blocking users = high cost) where misclassification costs are unequal.

Betweenness Centrality from scratch. Measures how often a node lies on shortest paths between other nodes. High betweenness indicates a "bridge" or connector node. Core idea: for each pair of nodes, count shortest paths passing through the target node, normalize by total paths between those nodes. Use when: identifying critical nodes in networks (e.g., bridges, key influencers).

Classical Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) from scratch. Non-linear dimensionality reduction: embed points in lower-dimensional space preserving pairwise distances. Core idea: convert distance matrix to inner-product matrix (double centering), then use eigendecomposition to find optimal low-rank embedding. Use when: visualizing high-dimensional data or embedding based on pairwise distances.

DBSCAN Clustering from scratch. Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise. Groups points that are close together (within eps distance) and have at least min_pts neighbors. Handles noise as outliers. Core idea: grow regions from dense points, merging overlapping regions. Use when: clusters have irregular shapes, density varies, or you need to identify noise.

Elbow Method + K-Means from scratch. K-means: iterative clustering that minimizes within-cluster inertia. Elbow method: plot inertia vs. k and find the knee (largest drop in inertia). Core idea: inertia decreases as k increases, but the rate of decrease flattens at the "true" k. Use when: choosing optimal k for k-means clustering without labels.

Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering from scratch. Bottom-up merging of clusters using distance linkage (single or complete). Produces a dendrogram (tree structure) of nested partitions. Cut at height k to get k clusters. Core idea: repeatedly merge two closest clusters until one remains. Use when: you want a hierarchy of clusters or need to explore multiple granularities.

Isolation Forest (Lite) Anomaly Detection from scratch. Ensemble of random isolation trees: points requiring fewer splits to isolate are likely anomalies (short average path length). Core idea: anomalies are isolated easily; normals require many splits. Anomaly score = average path length across trees (lower = anomaly). Use when: detecting outliers/anomalies without computing distances to all poin

Label Propagation for Community Detection from scratch. Iteratively propagate node labels throughout a graph: each node adopts the label held by most of its neighbors. Converges to stable partitions representing communities. Core idea: similar nodes (connected) naturally converge to same label; few cross-edges prevent full merging. Use when: detecting communities with minimal tuning or finding nat

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) from scratch. Two-class dimensionality reduction: find the linear projection that maximizes between-class variance relative to within-class variance. Core idea: compute class means, pooled within-class scatter, then solve generalized eigenvalue problem. Use when: projecting high-dimensional data to lower dims while preserving class separability.

Random Projection: Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma from scratch. Dimensionality reduction via random projection: project high-dimensional points onto a random subspace. Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantees: pairwise distances are approximately preserved (within factor 1±epsilon) with high probability. Core idea: random gaussian matrix of size target_dim × original_dim. Use when: fast approximate dimension

Silhouette Score from scratch. Measure of clustering quality: how similar a point is to its own cluster vs. other clusters. Score ranges from -1 (wrong cluster) to 1 (well-clustered). Computed per point as (b-a)/max(a,b), where a=avg distance to cluster members, b=min avg distance to other clusters. Use when: evaluating cluster quality or choosing optimal k for k-means.
Bayesian changepoint detection: find the point where mean shifts. Core claim: detected changepoint ≈ true location within tolerance.
Bayesian linear regression with conjugate prior. Posterior mean ≈ true βs; 95% credible interval covers them. Core claim: posterior mean ≈ true βs; 95% credible interval covers truth.

Beta-binomial: recover the planted overdispersion and beat the plain binomial. Counts with a random per-trial success probability p ~ Beta(α, β) are OVERDISPERSED relative to a binomial. Method-of-moments recovers (α, β) from the sample mean and variance (via the intra-class correlation ρ), and the beta-binomial log-likelihood at the recovered parameters beats the binomial at its MLE. BIC model selection picks the true polynomial degree. Fits polynomials of increasing degree by real least squares (Vandermonde normal equations solved with Gaussian elimination) and scores each with BIC = n·log(RSS/n) + k·log(n). BIC penalizes the extra parameters of over-fit models, so it selects the TRUE degree. Core claim: on data generated by a degree-1 model, argmin BIC == 1.
Chinese Restaurant Process (CRP): expected number of tables ≈ α·ln(n). Core claim: E[#tables] ≈ α·ln(n) within tolerance (planted α).
Dirichlet-Multinomial: posterior concentrates on true category probabilities as n grows. Core claim: posterior concentrates on true category probs as n grows.

Dirichlet stick-breaking process: samples probabilities that sum to 1. Weights sum→1; E[#active clusters] increases monotonically with α (concentration). Core claim: weights sum→1; E[#active clusters] increases with α.

Model evidence (via BIC) ranks the true generative model above the alternative. A FAIR comparison scores each model by BIC = −2·log L̂ + k·log n, evaluated at each model's own MLE with its own parameter count (Gaussian k=2, Exponential k=1). Lower BIC = better. On Gaussian data the Gaussian model earns the lower BIC. Core claim: BIC_true < BIC_alt.

Gaussian-process regression: the marginal likelihood peaks at the true lengthscale. The log marginal likelihood  log p(y|ℓ) = −½ yᵀK⁻¹y − ½ log|K| − n/2 log2π  (K the RBF kernel + noise) trades data-fit against complexity; scanned over ℓ it peaks near the lengthscale that GENERATED the data. Solved honestly with a Cholesky factorization (the yᵀK⁻¹y and log|K| both come from L), not a diagonal shor

Kalman filter + Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother: the backward pass lowers MSE. The filter estimates each state from the past only; the RTS smoother adds a backward pass that also uses the future, so on a random-walk state model it recovers the latent trajectory with strictly lower error IN EXPECTATION. Core claim: over many random-walk realizations the mean smoother MSE is below the mean filter

Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) Check for A/B Tests. In a valid A/B test, the allocation ratio should match the design (e.g., 50/50). A chi-square test on the observed counts detects when sample ratio deviates significantly. SRM flags data quality issues (e.g., bugs, bot filtering). We plant an SRM (skewed split) and a clean split; SRM caught vs clean passes.

CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data). In A/B tests, Y_post = metric post-treatment, Y_pre = metric pre-treatment. CUPED adjusted metric = Y_post - theta * Y_pre, where theta = Cov(Y_pre, Y_post) / Var(Y_pre). This removes covariate-driven noise, reducing the variance of the treatment effect estimate. We measure actual variance reduction from CUPED vs naive difference.

Difference-in-Differences (DiD). Two groups (treated and control) observed before and after treatment. Parallel trends assumption: absent treatment, both groups would have the same trend. DiD estimate = (Y_treated_post - Y_treated_pre) - (Y_control_post - Y_control_pre). We plant parallel trends and a treatment effect; DiD recovers the effect.

Instrumental Variable (IV) Estimation. Treatment T is endogenous: unobserved U affects both T and Y, creating bias. An instrument Z affects Y only through T (exogeneity), and Z is independent of U. IV estimate = Cov(Y, Z) / Cov(T, Z) (Wald estimator for binary Z, one endogenous T). We plant endogeneity and an valid instrument; IV recovers the true effect.

Interrupted Time Series (ITS) Segmented Regression. Time series with a pre-intervention trend; at a cutoff, intervention introduces a level change and/or slope change. Segmented regression detects both. Y = β0 + β1*t + β2*intervention + β3*t*intervention + noise. β2 = level change, β3 = slope change. We plant and recover both.

Placebo Test for Causal Inference. Under the null (no treatment effect), permuting treatment labels should destroy the measured effect. Under the alternative (true treatment effect), the effect persists under the true assignment but disappears under permuted assignments. We verify that true assignment recovers effect, permuted assignments do not.

Propensity Score Matching (PSM). Observational data is confounded: treatment assignment depends on observed traits. We estimate the propensity score P(treatment | confounders), then match treated and control units on their propensity score, creating pseudo-random assignment within strata. Naive OLS on the raw data will miss the true causal effect (or estimate it wrong). PSM recovers the true effec

Regression Discontinuity (RD). Treatment is assigned by a cutoff rule on a running variable: T=1 if X >= cutoff. There is a discontinuity in the outcome at the cutoff: E[Y | X=c+] - E[Y | X=c-] = ATE. We plant a cutoff effect and smooth underlying relationship; RD recovers the effect.

Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT). A sequential test that stops early: accumulate log-likelihood ratio for H0 vs H1. Stop when LR > threshold (accept H1) or LR < -threshold (accept H0). Compared to fixed-n testing at the same error rates, SPRT uses fewer observations on average. We verify that SPRT stops earlier than fixed-n while maintaining error rates.

Synthetic Control Method (Lite). A treated unit's outcome is compared to a weighted average of control units. Weights are chosen to match the treated unit's pre-intervention trends. Post-intervention, any gap between treated and synthetic control is the treatment effect. We plant pre-period trends and a treatment shock; SC recovers the gap.

Backpressure queue: refuses (non-blocking put_nowait) items when the bounded queue is full. Failure simulated: flood queue with 1000 items, cap=64; assert items are refused after the cap, peak depth ≤ cap, refused > 900.

Circuit breaker: opens after N failures, short-circuits further calls. Failure simulated: call function 100 times, it fails first 10 times; assert breaker opens after 10 failures, short-circuits remaining 90 calls, short-circuit count = 90.

CPU throttle: caps concurrent CPU-bound workers, refuses spawning past limit. Failure simulated: spawn 1000 CPU-bound workers with cap=4 concurrent; assert peak concurrent ≤ 4, >900 refused, workers stayed bounded.

Disk space watchdog: refuses writes when available space < threshold. Failure simulated: "fill" disk by tracking usage, attempt 1000 writes with cap=100MB; assert guard refuses writes when available < cap, peak usage ≤ cap.

File descriptor leak detector: caps open fds, refuses opens past limit. Failure simulated: open 1000 fds, assert the guard trips before exhaustion and peak fds never reach 1000 (caps at 64), refuses > 800.
Inode guard: refuses file creation past inode limit. Failure simulated: create 10000 files with cap=100; assert guard refuses creation when inode count reaches cap, peak ≤ cap.
Load shedding: drops excess requests to keep served load ≤ capacity. Failure simulated: submit 1000 requests with capacity=64; assert served ≤ 64, dropped > 900, peak served ≤ capacity.

Memory cap guard: refuses allocations past limit, keeps peak ≤ cap. Failure simulated: allocate 100 chunks × 10MB each (1GB total) with cap=256MB; assert guard raises MemoryError before peak reaches 1GB, and peak ≤ cap.

Tmp cleanup: auto-cleans temp files when usage exceeds quota. Failure simulated: create files until 200MB used, auto-cleanup kicks at 150MB; assert final size stays ≤ 150MB after cleanup + new creates, refused > 0.
Token bucket limiter: caps operation rate to tokens/sec. Failure simulated: issue 1000 ops over 2 sec with 10 tokens/sec cap; assert only ~20 ops granted, rest delayed/denied.

crash_loop_detector: count restarts in a sliding window; if threshold exceeded, flag crash-loop + stop restarting. Failure simulated: 6 restarts in 60 seconds (exceeds threshold of 5). Recovery asserted: crash_loop_flag is True; assert flag prevents further restarts.

graceful_shutdown_sigterm: install SIGTERM handler, save state gracefully, and exit. On receiving SIGTERM the handler writes a state file, then the process exits cleanly. The disaster test sends SIGTERM to a child process and asserts that the handler ran and the expected state was saved.

heartbeat_liveness: periodic heartbeat from a process; detector marks dead if none arrive by deadline. Failure simulated: heartbeat stops; deadline passes. Recovery asserted: detector marks dead; assert liveness_flag == False after timeout.

keepalive_daemon: a background thread pokes a keepalive file every interval; a watcher treats the process as alive only while pokes keep arriving within a timeout. Failure simulated (the real one): the daemon STOPS poking — the file goes stale. Recovery asserted: while poking, check_keepalive() is True; after the daemon stops and the timeout elapses, check_keepalive() flips to False — the stall is

pidfile_singleton: prevent multiple instances via pidfile; if pidfile exists and pid alive, refuse start. Failure simulated: second instance attempts to start. Recovery asserted: second instance is blocked; assert exception raised or lock_acquired == False.

readiness_vs_liveness: liveness = the process is running; readiness = it can serve requests. They are INDEPENDENT, and the point of the distinction is operational: a router must withhold traffic from an instance that is alive-but-unready, and drop one that is dead — while a liveness-only view would wrongly keep routing to a degraded instance. Failure simulated: a live instance degrades (unready),

restart_backoff: on repeated crashes, increase delay between restarts: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... (capped). Failure simulated: child crashes repeatedly. Recovery asserted: measure delays; assert they grow exponentially (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) up to cap.

supervised_child: spawn a child process; supervisor monitors and restarts on death. Failure simulated: child process dies. Recovery asserted: supervisor detects death and restarts; assert restart_count > 0.

watchdog_restart: a real watchdog supervises a child, restarts it on death up to a cap, then STOPS restarting and flags a crash-loop once the cap is exceeded. Failure simulated: the watchdog's OWN child is SIGKILL'd repeatedly (real deaths). Recovery asserted: the WATCHDOG (not the test) detects each death and restarts — assert the watchdog's restart counter reached the cap and a live child exists

zombie_reaper: spawn child; when child exits, reap it via SIGCHLD handler to prevent zombie. Failure simulated: spawn child, let it exit, parent doesn't wait immediately. Recovery asserted: SIGCHLD handler reaps child; assert no zombie remains (exitcode collected).
Backfill Range Pattern Fill gaps in time series or sequence. Assert: no gaps remain, existing records not duplicated.
Checkpoint/Resume Pattern Simulates crash inside batch processing, resumes from last checkpoint, asserts exactly-once processing and correct output.

Exactly-Once Deduplication Pattern Process a stream that may contain duplicates (e.g., from retry logic). Track processed record IDs in a journal, reject duplicates, assert that no duplicate record IDs are processed.

HEADLINE PATTERN: Idempotent ETL Step Simulates pipeline crash mid-transformation, resumes from checkpoint, asserts output is bit-identical and no duplicates despite replayed input. THE ONE LAW: An idempotent transform produces identical output when run once or replayed after crash. Counter-example: reading from offset N then restarting from offset 0 produces duplicates.

Lineage Tracking Pattern Track data provenance: which source records produced which output records. Assert: complete lineage (every output maps to at least one source), no dangling outputs, lineage is consistent.

Partition Management Pattern Manage partitions (e.g., date-based, range-based). Track which partitions are closed (immutable), which are open (mutable). Assert: no reprocessing closed partitions, exactly-once per partition.
Dead Letter Queue Pattern When processing fails, route to dead letter queue. Retry logic: retry 3 times, then move to DLQ. Assert: all records either processed or in DLQ, no lost records.

Replay-Safe Pattern Guarantee that replaying operations produces identical output. Assert: first run and replay produce same result, idempotency holds. Key: operations must be commutative and state-independent within a batch.
Schema Drift Detection Pattern Track expected schema. Detect when records deviate: - New fields added - Fields removed - Field types changed Assert: drift is detected and named explicitly.

Watermark Tracking Pattern Track the highest record timestamp processed. On resume, only process records with timestamp > watermark. Asserts: no reprocessing of old records, watermark monotonically increases.

append_only_audit: maintain an append-only audit log with hash chaining. Each entry hash includes the previous entry's hash (forming a chain). Tampering with an old entry breaks all subsequent hashes. Flip a byte in a past entry and verify the chain verification catches the break.
command_allowlist: enforce a whitelist of allowed commands. Only commands in the allowlist can be executed. Anything else is blocked.

immutable_audit: create an immutable audit log by sealing it with a cryptographic signature once written. After sealing, any tampering is detectable. Tamper with a sealed log and verify the signature breaks.
least_privilege_verify: grant only the minimum permissions needed for a task, then verify that unauthorized escalations are blocked.
permission_matrix: manage a permission matrix (users × resources × actions). Verify that a permission grants access. Tamper the matrix (flip a permission bit) and verify the tamper is detected.

priv_escalation_detect: detect privilege escalation by comparing user privileges across time. If a user gains a new privilege they didn't have before, flag it. This is state-change detection, not a static read.

rbac_check: enforce role-based access control. Verify that a user with role X can perform allowed action A, but cannot perform forbidden action B. Failure simulated: allowing a forbidden action. The checker must DENY the forbidden action AND ALLOW the permitted one.
session_record: record a user session (login, commands, logout). Verify the record is accurate and tamper-proof. Modify a logged command and verify tampering is detected.
sudo_self_body_guard: detect and block self-destructive sudo commands. Examples: rm -rf /, pkill -9 -u <self>, etc. The guard must allow safe sudo commands and block dangerous ones.

tamper_evident_chain: build a Merkle tree where each node's hash depends on its children. Any tampering with a leaf changes the root hash. Flip a byte in a leaf and verify the root hash validation fails.
binary_presence_check: verify that required binaries are installed and executable. Failure simulated: a required binary is missing or not executable. The checker must detect both conditions.

capability_probe: probe system capabilities (hardlinks, symlinks, sparse files, etc.) and record which are available. Mutate the system state (remove capability) and re-probe; verify the capability is no longer reported.

depgraph_resolve: resolve a dependency graph and detect cycles. Must name the cycle. A broken cycle detector would either miss it or crash. This one catches it and reports the exact names in the cycle.

deps_verify: verify a dependency manifest exists, all versions are pinned, and checksums match. Failure simulated: a malicious dep replaces a legitimate one with a different version under the same name. The verifier MUST catch it (version mismatch in actual vs expected).

dryrun_installer: perform a dry-run installation (no actual modifications), verify it would succeed, then do a real installation and verify the system state changed correctly. The dry-run must NOT modify the system; a broken dry-run would leave side effects.

env_diff: compare two environment dictionaries (env vars) and report differences. Failure simulated: missing a key variable, wrong value, or extra variable. The differ must accurately report all three types of changes.

lockfile_hash_integrity: store dep checksums in a lockfile; verify them; tamper one and detect the break. Each entry is hashed (SHA256 of the dep content). Tampering with the content breaks the hash. A naive verifier that just reads hashes from the tampered file would miss the breach — this one recomputes and compares.

path_sanity: verify that required binaries exist in PATH and are at expected locations. Failure simulated: a binary is moved/deleted, or a malicious binary is injected earlier in PATH. The checker must detect the absence or unexpected location.

reproducible_build_check: build twice with identical inputs, verify byte-for-byte output matches. Then mutate one input and verify the build differs. This detects non-determinism and ensures builds are truly deterministic.

version_constraint_solve: given constraints {name: constraint_str}, resolve to valid versions or raise ValueError if unsatisfiable. Must reject conflicting constraints and accept compatible ones. A naive solver might ignore conflicts or get the logic wrong.

atomic_snapshot: take an atomic snapshot of a file at a point in time. Failure simulated: snapshot a live file, modify the original, verify snapshot is unchanged. The snapshot is taken via temp-write + rename, ensuring atomicity. Recovery asserted: snapshot holds the original bytes exactly; subsequent modifications to the source don't affect the snapshot. Pattern's own snapshot function is called.

atomic_write_temp_rename: write atomically by writing to a temp file, then atomic rename. Failure simulated (the REAL one): a writer is SIGKILL'd AFTER the temp is fully written but BEFORE the rename. Recovery asserted: the target is left completely untouched — still the intact OLD content, never torn/partial/new. That is the all-or-nothing guarantee of temp+rename, and the assert FAILS on a non-a

checksum_corruption_detect: detect corruption via checksum mismatch. Failure simulated: write file + compute checksum; corrupt a byte in the file; recompute checksum and assert it differs (corruption detected). Recovery asserted: honest checksum detects single-byte flip; a no-op check (len, first byte) would miss it. Pattern's own checksum function must be called.

cow_backup: an independent point-in-time backup that survives later source corruption. NAME DISCLOSURE (honest): this is an EAGER FULL COPY (read all bytes → temp → atomic rename), NOT block-level copy-on-write. It delivers the same USER-FACING guarantee a CoW backup gives — the backup is fully independent of the source, so corrupting the source cannot touch it — WITHOUT the block-sharing space/ti

dir_tree_diff: compute a diff between two directory trees (file presence, size, content hash). Failure simulated: create two similar trees; modify one file; diff trees and assert the difference is detected (changed file flagged, unchanged files not). Recovery asserted: diff correctly identifies added, removed, modified, and unchanged files. Pattern's own diff function is called.

disk_full_write_guard: refuse writes when disk space is exhausted or quota exceeded. Failure simulated: attempt to write past disk quota; guard should refuse; existing data remains intact. Guard trips BEFORE exhaustion, not after. Recovery asserted: write is blocked when it would exceed quota; existing data untouched; no partial/torn writes. Pattern's own guard function is called.

fsync_durability: write data then fsync to flush it to stable storage before returning. Failure defended against: process/power death after write() but before the OS flushes the page cache — the data would be lost on a crash without fsync. restore_from_backup: restore a file from backup after corruption/deletion. Failure simulated: backup a file; delete/corrupt the original; restore from backup; assert the original is recovered to exact byte-for-byte match. Recovery asserted: restored file == backed-up file; no data loss; corruption is undone. Pattern's own restore function is called, not the test scaffold.

safe_delete_trash: delete files to trash (not permanent deletion). Failure simulated: delete a file via trash move; assert file is gone from original location but recoverable from trash. Prevent permanent data loss via trash buffer. Recovery asserted: file removed from source; file exists in trash; can be restored from trash. Pattern's own delete-to-trash function is called.

symlink_escape_guard: refuse to create symlinks that escape the root directory. Failure simulated: attempt to create symlinks that point outside root (escape attack); assert the guard refuses it. Allow symlinks within root. Recovery asserted: escape attempts are blocked; safe symlinks are created; path resolution proves the target is within root or denied. Pattern's own guard function is called.
counter_gauge_histogram: implement counter, gauge, and histogram metric types.
heartbeat_miss_alert: detect heartbeat/watchdog timeouts.
metric_export: export metrics in standard formats.

p2_percentile: P2 algorithm (Jain & Chlamtac 1985) for online percentile estimation. The P2 estimator keeps only FIVE markers (O(1) memory) and never stores the stream. The middle marker q[2] tracks the desired p-quantile; the estimate is read from the markers, NOT from a retained copy of the data.
rate_calc: calculate rate (e.g., requests per second) from counter.
sliding_aggregate: compute rolling aggregates (sum, avg, min, max).
slo_error_budget: track error budget against SLO.
threshold_alert: fire alerts when metrics cross thresholds.
uptime_calc: calculate uptime percentage from events.
zscore_anomaly: detect anomalies using z-score.
load_avg_read: Parse /proc/loadavg (1min, 5min, 15min load averages). THE ONE LAW: Parse exact values, fail on missing fields.
memory_pressure: Parse /proc/pressure/memory for PSI (Pressure Stall Info) metrics. THE ONE LAW: Parse exact pressure values, fail on incomplete data.
mount_disk_usage: Parse mount output and extract filesystem usage. THE ONE LAW: Parse real df-style output, assert exact usage percentages.
open_fd_count: Count open file descriptors from /proc/[pid]/fd. THE ONE LAW: Parse directory listing, assert exact count matches directory size. Portable fallback on non-Linux.
orphan_detect: Identify orphaned processes (parent pid doesn't exist). THE ONE LAW: Parse tree, identify orphans by ppid not in known pids, return exact list.

proc_parse_portable: Parse /proc-style process info, portable across platforms. Handles missing /proc gracefully; tests against synthetic data regardless. THE ONE LAW: Simulate parse failure on malformed data, assert it's caught.

process_tree: Build process tree from /proc-style data, re-parent orphans to ppid=1. THE ONE LAW: Parse process list with dead-parent process, assert it's re-parented to 1. Anti-fake rule 2: Failure case must assert orphan STAYS orphaned without the fix.
resource_usage: Extract memory/CPU metrics from /proc/[pid]/status. THE ONE LAW: Parse real data, assert exact values; simulate missing fields, assert error.
top_n_by_resource: Rank processes by a resource metric (RSS, CPU, etc.). THE ONE LAW: Sort and rank, assert exact ordering; simulate unsorted input.
uptime_read: Parse /proc/uptime to extract uptime in seconds and idle time. THE ONE LAW: Parse exact values, assert single clock (no time() calls during parse).

Failure simulated: launch two processes; first acquires and holds, second tries non-blocking acquire, gets EWOULDBLOCK, then waits with a timeout. Failure simulated: MANY processes each do read-the-whole-file → add their line → write it back (a read-modify-write, the classic lost-update race). deadlock_timeout: detect and break potential deadlocks with a timeout mechanism. Failure simulated: two threads try to acquire locks in opposite order (A: lock1→lock2, B: lock2→lock1), creating a cycle. Without timeouts, this deadlocks forever.
